cases.title: Dopamine neuron firing rate and reward size
cases.context: A study was reported concerning how midbrain dopamine neurons (cells in the ventral tegmental area that respond to rewards) code the size of a reward. Ten neurons were recorded in a monkey, and each neuron was tested with a different volume of juice in milliliters (mL). The firing rate in spikes per second (spikes/s) was measured in the 200 milliseconds (ms) after the juice was delivered. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R.
tasks: (i) Find the linear regression relationship between reward volume (independent variable) and firing rate (dependent variable). Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
(ii) Using only your calculations for Part (i), what firing rate does the line give for a reward of 0.7 mL?
cases.symbols: \(n\) (number of neurons), \(x\) (reward volume, mL), \(y\) (firing rate, spikes/s), \(b\) (least-squares slope, spikes/s per mL), \(a\) (least-squares intercept, spikes/s), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(D\) (shared denominator).

steps.title: Collect the sums
steps.words: The least-squares formulas need only these five numbers, read from the bottom row of the table.

steps.title: Calculate the shared denominator
steps.words: Both the slope and the intercept formulas divide by this quantity, in mL².

steps.title: Calculate the slope
steps.words: The slope is the estimated increase in mean firing rate per milliliter of juice, in spikes/s per mL.

steps.title: Calculate both sample means
steps.words: The least-squares line passes through the point of means (0.6 mL, 8.93 spikes/s).

steps.title: Calculate the intercept from the means
steps.words: Carry the unrounded slope into this step, because rounding b first would shift the intercept.

steps.title: Check the intercept with the full formula
steps.words: Both routes give the same intercept, in spikes/s.

steps.title: Write the line and use it at 0.7 mL
steps.words: The line gives a mean firing rate of about 9.729 spikes/s for a 0.7 mL reward. This volume lies inside the range of the data, so the line can be used there.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares line is \(\hat y=4.135+7.992x\). Mean firing rate is estimated to rise by about 7.99 spikes/s for each additional milliliter of juice, and the line gives about 9.729 spikes/s at 0.7 mL.

cases.title: Morning cortisol and hours of sleep
cases.context: Researchers interested in stress did a study to evaluate whether the stress hormone cortisol is related to sleep. Ten healthy adults wore a wrist actigraph (a motion sensor that estimates sleep) for one night, and the hours of sleep were recorded. The next morning the salivary cortisol concentration in nanomoles per liter (nmol/L) was measured 30 minutes after waking. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R.
tasks: (i) Calculate the slope b of the regression line of cortisol on hours of sleep.
(ii) Calculate the standard error of the estimate \(s_{y|x}\) (the SD of the points about the regression line).
(iii) Using only your calculations for Parts (i) and (ii), calculate the standard errors \(s_b\) and \(s_a\). Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
cases.symbols: \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate, nmol/L), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(b\) (slope, nmol/L per hour), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope, nmol/L per hour), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept, nmol/L), \(\bar x\) (mean hours of sleep), \(n\) (sample size).

steps.title: Calculate the mean of x and both sample variances
steps.words: These come from the totals in the bottom row of the table.

steps.title: Calculate the slope
general: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}
steps.words: The slope is negative, so morning cortisol is lower in the adults who slept longer.

steps.title: Square the pieces inside the shortcut
steps.words: The first term is the total variance of y. The second term is the part of that variance explained by the line.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: The factor (n−1)/(n−2) turns the n−1 denominators of the sample variances into the n−2 denominator that regression needs. The points scatter about the line with an SD of about 1.063 nmol/L.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the slope
steps.words: The slope is uncertain by about 0.2724 nmol/L per hour.

steps.title: Evaluate the bracket for the intercept
steps.words: The second term grows with the distance between the mean of x and x = 0, where the intercept is defined.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the intercept
steps.words: The intercept is uncertain by about 1.816 nmol/L.

steps.title: Check with the residual sum of squares
steps.words: Subtracting the fitted value from each observed value and squaring gives a residual sum of squares of 9.0408. This direct route gives the same scatter as the shortcut, so the standard errors are confirmed.

cases.conclusion: The slope is \(b=-2.29\) nmol/L per hour. The scatter about the line is \(s_{y|x}=1.063\) nmol/L, with \(s_b=0.2724\) nmol/L per hour and \(s_a=1.816\) nmol/L.

cases.title: Hearing threshold and years of noise exposure
cases.context: A study was reported concerning hearing loss in workers at a metal stamping plant. For each of 10 workers, the number of years of work on the factory floor was recorded. The hearing threshold (the quietest tone that the worker could detect) was then measured at 4 kilohertz (kHz) with pure-tone audiometry, in decibels hearing level (dB HL). Audiometers step in 5 dB, so every threshold is a multiple of 5. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: (i) Find the linear regression relationship between years of noise exposure (independent variable) and hearing threshold (dependent variable).
(ii) Calculate the standard errors \(s_b\) and \(s_a\). Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
(iii) Based on your calculations for b, is the trend between hearing threshold and years of noise exposure statistically significant?
(iv) What are the 95% confidence intervals for the slope and for the intercept of the line of means?

(v) Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: Mean hearing threshold does not change linearly with years of noise exposure in this population of workers, so the slope of the line of means is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean hearing threshold changes linearly with years of noise exposure, so the slope of the line of means is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(x\) (noise exposure, years), \(y\) (hearing threshold, dB HL), \(S_{xx},S_{yy},S_{xy}\) (sums of squared and cross deviations), \(b\) (sample slope, dB HL per year), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope), \(a\) (sample intercept), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\alpha_{LOM}\) (population intercept), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

steps.title: Calculate both means
steps.words: The regression line passes through the point of means (14.8 years, 25 dB HL).

steps.title: Calculate the deviation sums
steps.words: These equal Σ(x−x̄)², Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) and Σ(y−ȳ)². They come from the totals in the bottom row of the table.

steps.title: Calculate the slope
general: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}
steps.words: The slope is the estimated rise in mean threshold for each additional year on the factory floor, in dB HL per year.

steps.title: Calculate the intercept
steps.words: Carry the unrounded slope into this step. The line is ŷ = 6.439 + 1.254x.

steps.title: Calculate the sample variances
steps.words: These two variances feed the shortcut formula for the scatter about the line.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: The factor (n−1)/(n−2) turns the n−1 denominators of the sample variances into the n−2 denominator that regression needs. The points scatter about the line with an SD of about 5.031 dB HL.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the slope
steps.words: The slope is uncertain by about 0.1863 dB HL per year.

steps.title: Evaluate the bracket for the intercept
steps.words: The second term grows with the distance between the mean of x and x = 0, where the intercept is defined.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the intercept
steps.words: The intercept is uncertain by about 3.183 dB HL.

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the t test for the slope of a regression line. The null hypothesis states that mean hearing threshold does not change with years of noise exposure.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis β = 0, so the statistic is the slope divided by its standard error.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two coefficients, the intercept and the slope, are estimated from the data.

steps.title: Find the 0.05 critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The size of the statistic exceeds the cutoff, so the null hypothesis of no trend is rejected.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: Row 8, column 0.001 prints 5.041. The statistic exceeds the largest printed cutoff, so P < 0.001.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the slope
steps.words: The interval does not contain 0, which agrees with the test.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the intercept
steps.words: This interval covers the plausible values of mean hearing threshold at x = 0, in dB HL.

cases.conclusion: The line is \(\hat y=6.439+1.254x\). The statistic t = 6.733 with ν = 8 exceeds \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\) and \(t_{0.001}(8)=5.041\), so the trend between hearing threshold and years of noise exposure is statistically significant (P < 0.001). The 95% confidence interval for the slope is 0.8246 to 1.684 dB HL per year and does not contain 0. For the intercept it is −0.9003 to 13.78 dB HL. Workers who had spent more years in the noise needed louder tones before they could hear them, by about 1.25 dB for each extra year.

cases.title: Mental rotation speed in younger and older adults
cases.context: In a study looking at mental rotation (deciding whether two drawn objects are the same when one has been turned through an angle), 12 younger adults and 12 older adults were each tested at one rotation angle in degrees (deg). The mean response time in milliseconds (ms) for correct answers was recorded for each subject. A separate regression of response time on angle was fitted to each group in R with summary(lm(RT.ms ~ Angle.deg)), and the coefficient tables are shown below. The residual standard error was 41.29 ms on 10 degrees of freedom for the older group (multiple R-squared 0.9727) and 44.29 ms on 10 degrees of freedom for the younger group (multiple R-squared 0.9513). The same 12 angles were used in both groups.
tasks: (i) Is there a difference between the two groups in the slope of response time against angle (the extra time needed for each additional degree of rotation)? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
(ii) Apply the corresponding test to the intercepts.

hypotheses.nullWords: Response time rises with rotation angle at the same rate in older and younger adults, so the two lines of means have equal slopes.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which response time rises with rotation angle is different in older and younger adults.

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the two-regression-line t test. Both slopes are significant on their own (t = 18.86 and 13.97), so the comparison is meaningful.

steps.words: Keep the order older minus younger throughout.

steps.title: Apply the corresponding intercept test
steps.words: Replacing slopes by intercepts in the same formula gives t = 5.481, which exceeds 3.850, the 0.001 cutoff of row 20. The intercepts also differ, so older adults are slower even when the two objects are not rotated at all.

cases.conclusion: The statistic t = 2.643 with ν = 20 exceeds \(t_{0.05}(20)=2.086\) and \(t_{0.02}(20)=2.528\) but not \(t_{0.01}(20)=2.845\), so there is a difference between the slopes (0.01 < P < 0.02). Response time rises faster with angle in older adults (4.1747 ms per deg) than in younger adults (3.3167 ms per deg).

cases.title: Amygdala response to fearful faces and trait anxiety
cases.context: In a study looking at mood and threat processing, 10 adults completed a trait anxiety questionnaire (a score from 20 to 80, where higher means more anxious). Each adult then viewed fearful and neutral faces during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and the amygdala response was recorded as the percent signal change (%) for fearful faces compared with neutral faces. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: (i) Calculate the correlation (Pearson coefficient) between amygdala response and trait anxiety score.
(ii) Is the correlation different from zero? Use a significance level of α = 0.05 for your inference, then give the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear relationship between amygdala response and trait anxiety score in the population, so the population correlation is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Amygdala response and trait anxiety score are linearly related in the population, so the population correlation is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(r\) (sample correlation coefficient), \(\rho\) (population correlation), \(b\) (slope), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate the deviation totals from the sums
steps.words: The totals in the bottom row of the table give the three deviation totals that the correlation needs.

steps.title: Calculate r from the deviation totals
steps.words: The units cancel, so r has no units.

steps.title: Check with the slope relation
steps.words: The slope relation gives the same value, and r has the same sign as b.

steps.title: Square r
steps.words: About 79.07% of the variation in amygdala response is accounted for by the linear relationship with trait anxiety score.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: The null hypothesis states that the population correlation is zero. This statistic equals the slope statistic b divided by its standard error for the same data.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis of zero correlation. Row 8, column 0.001 prints 5.041. The statistic exceeds the largest printed cutoff, so P < 0.001.

steps.title: Interpret r
steps.words: A value this close to +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, so adults with higher trait anxiety tend to show a larger amygdala response to fearful faces. A correlation does not show that one causes the other.

cases.conclusion: The correlation is r = 0.8892. The statistic t = 5.497 with ν = 8 exceeds \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\) and \(t_{0.001}(8)=5.041\), so the correlation is different from zero (P < 0.001).

cases.title: Resting alpha power and vigilance reaction time
cases.context: Researchers interested in attention did a study to evaluate whether resting brain rhythms are related to vigilance. For each of 10 students, 5 minutes of eyes-closed electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded, and the alpha power (the strength of the 8 to 12 Hz rhythm over the back of the head) was calculated in microvolts squared (μV²). Each student then completed a 10-minute vigilance task, and the mean reaction time in milliseconds (ms) was recorded. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: (i) Calculate the correlation (Pearson coefficient) between reaction time and alpha power.
(ii) Is the correlation different from zero? Please state how you reached your conclusions.

(iii) Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear relationship between reaction time and resting alpha power in the population, so the population correlation is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Reaction time and resting alpha power are linearly related in the population, so the population correlation is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(r\) (sample correlation coefficient), \(\rho\) (population correlation), \(b\) (slope), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate the deviation totals from the sums
steps.words: The totals in the bottom row of the table give the three deviation totals that the correlation needs.

steps.title: Calculate r from the deviation totals
steps.words: The units cancel, so r has no units.

steps.title: Check with the slope relation
steps.words: The slope relation gives the same value, and r has the same sign as b.

steps.title: Square r
steps.words: About 26.32% of the variation in reaction time is accounted for by the linear relationship with alpha power.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: The null hypothesis states that the population correlation is zero. This statistic equals the slope statistic b divided by its standard error for the same data.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: Do not reject the null hypothesis of zero correlation. The statistic is below the 0.05 cutoff in row 8, so P is greater than 0.05 and no stricter column needs to be checked.

steps.title: Interpret r
steps.words: The sample correlation is negative and moderate in size. With only 10 students a value of this size can easily arise by chance when the population correlation is zero, so the sign of r is not interpreted.

cases.conclusion: The correlation is r = −0.5131. The size of the statistic t = −1.691 with ν = 8 is below \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\), so the correlation is not shown to be different from zero (P > 0.05). This small study found no convincing evidence that students with stronger resting alpha rhythms respond faster or slower in the vigilance task.

questions.stem: Ten dopamine neurons were each tested with a different juice volume x (mL), and the firing rate y (spikes/s) was recorded. The totals are \(\sum x=6\), \(\sum y=89.3\), \(\sum x^2=4.8\) and \(\sum xy=63.17\). What is the least-squares slope b?
questions.why: The slope is (10·63.17 − 6·89.3)/(10·4.8 − 6²) = 95.9/12 = 7.992. Leaving (Σx)² out of the denominator gives 1.998, and dividing Σxy by Σx² gives 13.16, which forces the line through the origin.
equations: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

questions.stem: In the study of morning cortisol against hours of sleep (n = 10), \(s_y^2=9.8782\), \(s_x^2=1.6917\) and \(b=-2.2903\) nmol/L per hour. What is the standard error of the estimate \(s_{y|x}\)?
questions.why: s_y|x = √[(9/8)(9.8782 − 8.8737)] = √1.13 = 1.063 nmol/L. Forgetting the root gives 1.13, dropping the 9/8 factor gives 1.002, and inverting it gives 0.9449.

questions.stem: Movement time (ms) was regressed on index of difficulty (bits) for 11 subjects in a reaching task. Which quantity describes how far a typical subject's movement time lies from the regression line?
options: The standard error of the slope \(s_b\)
The standard error of the intercept \(s_a\)
The standard error of the estimate \(s_{y|x}\)
questions.why: The standard error of the estimate is the SD of the points about the line, in ms. The values s_b and s_a describe the uncertainty of the two coefficients, and s_y measures spread about the mean, which ignores the line.

questions.stem: For 10 factory workers, the regression of hearing threshold (dB HL) on years of noise exposure gives \(b=1.254\) dB HL per year with \(s_b=0.1863\), and \(a=6.439\) dB HL with \(s_a=3.183\). The scatter about the line is \(s_{y|x}=5.031\) dB HL. What is the t statistic for the trend?
questions.why: t = b/s_b = 1.254/0.1863 = 6.733. Dividing b by s_y|x gives 0.2493, and a/s_a = 2.023 tests the intercept, not the trend.

questions.stem: Cold-water tolerance time was regressed on catastrophizing score for 12 volunteers, and the slope gave |t| = 2.686. Which printed two-tailed cutoff at α = 0.05 is the correct one for this test?
questions.why: A regression line estimates two coefficients, so ν = n − 2 = 10 and the cutoff is 2.228. Because 2.686 exceeds 2.228, the trend is significant at the 0.05 level.

questions.stem: For 10 adults, the regression of indifference point ($) on delay (weeks) predicts \(\hat y=59.025\) dollars at a delay of 14 weeks, with \(s_{\hat y}=1.413\) and \(s_{Y_{new}}=4.23\) dollars. What is the lower endpoint of the 95% Confidence Interval for the mean indifference point at 14 weeks?
questions.why: 59.025 − 2.306(1.413) = 55.77 dollars with ν = 8. Using s_Ynew gives 49.27, which is the interval for one adult. Using 1.96 gives 56.26 and using ν = 10 gives 55.88.

questions.stem: Heart-rate variability (RMSSD, ms) was regressed on perceived stress score for 10 office workers. A clinician wants a range that should contain the RMSSD of one new worker with a stress score of 20. Which statement is correct?
options: Use \(\hat y\pm t_{0.05}(\nu)s_{Y_{new}}\), which is wider than the interval for the mean because it adds the scatter of individuals about the line.
Use \(\hat y\pm t_{0.05}(\nu)s_{\hat y}\), because one worker is a sample of size 1 from the line of means.
Use \(b\pm t_{0.05}(\nu)s_b\), because the slope carries all the uncertainty at a score of 20.
Use \(\hat y\pm t_{0.05}(\nu)s_{y|x}\), because the uncertainty in the line does not matter for one worker.
questions.why: A single observation varies about the line of means with variance s²_y|x, and the line itself is uncertain with variance s²_ŷ. The two variances add, so the interval for one worker is wider than the interval for the mean.

questions.stem: Response time (ms) was regressed on rotation angle (deg) separately for 12 older and 12 younger adults. R gave a slope of 4.1747 (Std. Error 0.2214) for the older group and 3.3167 (Std. Error 0.2374) for the younger group. What is the t statistic for the difference between the slopes?
questions.why: The difference is 0.858 and its standard error is √(0.2214² + 0.2374²) = 0.3246, so t = 2.643 with ν = 20. Adding the two standard errors without squaring gives 1.87, and using only one standard error gives 3.875.

questions.stem: For 10 adults, amygdala response y (%) and trait anxiety score x give \(\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=16.569\), \(\sum(x-\bar x)^2=992.9\) and \(\sum(y-\bar y)^2=0.34969\). Calculate the correlation (Pearson coefficient).
questions.why: r = 16.569/√(992.9·0.34969) = 0.8892. The value 0.7907 is r², and 0.01669 is the slope b, which divides by Σ(x − x̄)² only.

questions.stem: Resting alpha power and vigilance reaction time in 10 students give r = −0.5131, so t = −1.691 with ν = 8, and \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\). Which conclusion is correct?
options: The correlation is negative, so stronger alpha power causes faster reactions.
The correlation is different from zero, because r is farther from 0 than 0.5.
The correlation is not shown to be different from zero (P > 0.05), so the data do not establish a linear relationship.
The data prove that alpha power and reaction time are unrelated.
questions.why: The size of t, 1.691, is below 2.306, so the null hypothesis of zero correlation is not rejected. Failing to reject does not prove that there is no relationship, and a correlation never shows causation.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Every hand case carries full precision between steps and prints 7 significant figures, so a last printed digit can differ by one unit from arithmetic done with the printed values.
Critical values were read from the printed t table (sources/tables/t_table.pdf, page 1), rows 8, 10 and 20. No row had to be bracketed.

n18-b-mental-rotation-age stores the two summary(lm()) coefficient tables in `table` (lm() row, Estimate, Std. Error, t value, Pr(>|t|)), the way the ref case s18-plutonian-males stores R output. The residual standard errors and R-squared values are in the context. The hand calculation uses the printed (rounded) estimates. The invented raw data are in check_session18b.py.

n18-b-mental-rotation-age reuses the ref value key names nM, bM, sbM (group 1, here the older adults) and nF, bF, sbF, femaleXbar, femaleSx (group 2, here the younger adults). Its t lies between the 0.02 and 0.01 columns, so it carries critical002 and an added key critical01.

n18-b-coldpressor-catastrophizing lands between the 0.05 and 0.02 columns (0.02 < P < 0.05) and carries the added key critical002 next to the ref keys. n18-b-alpha-vigilance does not reject (P > 0.05).

Raw-data tables have a first label column (Neuron, Subject, Worker, ...) and a Total row whose cells are numbers. The ref line case has no label column and writes the totals as strings such as 'Total 369'.

The s18syx, s18slope, s18predict and s18corr cases start from raw pairs and sums, so they have extra opening steps before the steps of the matching ref case. In the s18syx cases syxRaw, sbRaw and saRaw come from the residual sum of squares and equal syx, sb and sa.
The step-level table lookup uses the key `classTable`, as in the ref cases.

Wording review. Each hand-case context now carries the homework sentences "The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. In answering the questions below, DO NOT use R." The summations are still the Total row of the table. Negative numbers in running text use the minus sign − as the reference cases do. check_session18b.py allows that one colon in the context.
